propositions.text: The Applicant seeks judicial review of the Officer's refusal of her study permit application under section 216(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations.
propositions.quote: The Applicant seeks judicial review of the decision of an immigration officer [Officer] of the Visa Section of the Embassy of Canada in Abu Dhabi refusing her application for a study permit pursuant to section 216(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant seeks judicial review of the Officer's refusal of her study permit application under section 216(1).

propositions.text: The Officer's decision was unreasonable on all three bases for concluding the Applicant would not leave Canada after her stay.
propositions.quote: The Applicant asserts that the Officer’s decision was unreasonable in relation to all three bases upon which the Officer concluded that the Officer was not satisfied that the Applicant would leave Canada at the end of her stay.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer's decision was unreasonable on all three bases for refusal.

propositions.text: The Officer's decision is unreasonable and judicial review is granted.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I find that the Officer’s decision is unreasonable and as a result, the application for judicial review shall be granted.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's decision unreasonable and grants judicial review.

propositions.text: The Applicant is a 28-year-old Filipino citizen with family and land in the Philippines.
propositions.quote: The Applicant is a 28-year-old citizen of the Philippines. Her father, step-mother, two half-brothers and a half-sister all continue to reside in the Philippines, where the Applicant also owns land.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant is a 28-year-old Filipino citizen with family and land in the Philippines.

propositions.text: The Applicant graduated in 2014 with a BSc in Tourism and worked in non-tourism jobs in the Philippines and Dubai.
propositions.quote: The Applicant graduated with a Bachelor of Science in Tourism from Abra Valley College in Bangeud, Philippines in 2014 and since that time, she has worked in various non-tourism jobs in the Philippines and Dubai.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant graduated in 2014 with a BSc in Tourism and worked in non-tourism jobs in Philippines and Dubai.

propositions.text: In February 2021, the Applicant was accepted into a two-year diploma program at Seneca College in Toronto with tuition about $32,000.
propositions.quote: In February 2021, the Applicant was accepted into a two-year diploma program at Seneca College in Toronto, Ontario in Tourism – Services Management – Travel Services Specialization, with total tuition fees estimated to be approximately $32,000.00.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant was accepted into a two-year diploma at Seneca College with tuition about $32,000.

propositions.text: In March 2021, the Applicant applied for a study permit with a Statement of Purpose and supporting documents.
propositions.quote: In March 2021, the Applicant submitted an application for a study permit. Included with her application was a Statement of Purpose, in which the Applicant explained her rationale for enrolling in the diploma program at Seneca College, as well as numerous letters of support and other supporting documentation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant applied for a study permit with a Statement of Purpose and supporting documents.

propositions.text: The Officer refused the study permit because of concerns about personal assets, family ties, and purpose of visit.
propositions.quote: By letter dated May 20, 2021, the Officer advised the Applicant that her study permit application was refused as the Officer was not satisfied that she would leave Canada at the end of her stay based on: (a) her personal assets and financial status; (b) her family ties in Canada and in her country of residence; and (c) the purpose of her visit.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer refused the study permit due to concerns about personal assets, family ties, and purpose of visit.

propositions.text: The sole issue is whether the Officer's decision was reasonable.
propositions.quote: The sole issue raised on this application is whether the Officer’s decision was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the sole issue is whether the Officer's decision was reasonable.

propositions.text: The standard of review is reasonableness, with no exceptions raised or applicable.
propositions.quote: The parties submit, and I agree, that the presumptive standard of review is reasonableness. No exceptions to that presumption have been raised nor apply [see Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 23, 25].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness, with no exceptions raised or applicable.

propositions.text: A reasonable decision is transparent, intelligible, justified, and based on a rational chain of analysis.
propositions.quote: According to the standard of reasonableness, a reviewing Court must determine whether the decision under review, including both its rationale and outcome, is transparent, intelligible and justified. A reasonable decision is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker [see Vavilov, supra at paras 15, 85].

paragraphs.summary: The court explains a reasonable decision is transparent, intelligible, justified, and based on rational analysis.

propositions.text: Officers' reasons for study permit refusals need not be comprehensive but must allow understanding and justification.
propositions.quote: In the case of a study permit application, this Court has recognized that decisions of an officer need not be comprehensive and an officer may provide brief or even limited reasons. However, they must be sufficient to understand the reasons an application was refused and allow the Court to find they provide the justification, transparency, and intelligibility required of a reasonable decision [see Aghaalikhani v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1080 at para 16; Ekpenyong v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2019 FC 1245 at para 13; Peiro v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 1146 at para 15].

paragraphs.summary: The court states officers' reasons for study permit refusals need not be comprehensive but must allow understanding and justification.

propositions.text: The Officer's decision is mainly in GCMS notes explaining the three bases for refusal.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s decision is largely contained in their Global Case Management System [GCMS] notes, which form part of the reasons for decision. The GCMS notes particularize the Officer’s rationale for their three bases for concluding that the Officer was not satisfied that the Applicant would leave Canada at the end of her stay. I will deal with each basis in turn.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Officer's decision is mainly in GCMS notes explaining the three bases for refusal.

propositions.text: The Officer found the Applicant's financial documents did not show sufficient or available funds and studies were not a reasonable expense.
propositions.quote: Taking the applicant's plan of studies into account, the documentation provided in support of the applicant's financial situation does not demonstrate that funds would be sufficient or available. I am not satisfied that the proposed studies would be a reasonable expense.

propositions.text: The Officer noted a relative offered assistance but lacked details on family size and income.
propositions.quote: An offer of assistance has been provided by the applicant’s relative however, while relative show [sic] some funds, there is no indication of size of family being supported by this income nor information on employment/income.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found the Applicant's financial documents insufficient and assistance from a relative lacked supporting details.

propositions.text: The Applicant submitted proof of tuition payment and a lawyer's letter confirming trust funds for further tuition.
propositions.quote: However, included in the documentation submitted by the Applicant in support of her study permit was proof of payment of $8,013.46 to Seneca College towards her tuition and a letter from her aunt and uncle’s lawyer confirming that he was holding an additional $16,078.18 in trust for the payment of further tuition.

propositions.text: These funds cover almost all two-year tuition and exceed first-year requirements.
propositions.quote: This represented proof of secured funds for the payment of almost the entirety of her two-year tuition and more than simply proof of financial support for the first year of her studies as required by the document checklist provided by IRCC.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant submitted proof of tuition payment and trust funds covering almost all tuition.

propositions.text: The Applicant submitted letters from aunt and uncle and their financial planner and accountant confirming financial support and resources.
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Applicant submitted a letter of support from her aunt and uncle confirming that they would support her during her studies and provide her with room and board. The Applicant also submitted a letter from the aunt and uncle’s financial planner (with whom they had been working for over a decade) who manages the uncle’s RRIF and who builds and updates their financial plan. The financial planner confirmed that the aunt and uncle have the necessary resources to financially support the Applicant during her studies at Seneca College. A further letter was provided from the aunt and uncle’s accountant, who has been providing them with accounting services for 14 and 25 years respectively. The accountant also certified that the aunt and uncle have sufficient funds available to support the Applicant during her studies at Seneca College. Multiple bank account statements for the aunt and uncle over a period of many months showing total balances in excess of $15,000.00 were also provided.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant submitted letters and bank statements confirming aunt and uncle's financial support and resources.

propositions.text: Decision-makers must address relevant evidence contradicting their findings; failure may indicate erroneous fact-finding.
propositions.quote: A decision-maker is required to address relevant evidence if such evidence goes directly to contradict their findings. The Court may infer that a decision-maker has made an erroneous finding of fact without regard to the evidence from a failure to mention in the reasons evidence that is relevant to the finding and which points to a different conclusion [see Kaur v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 934 at para 40; Cepeda-Gutierrez v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] FCJ No 1425 at para 15].

propositions.text: The Officer failed to mention evidence proving tuition paid, funds held in trust, and financial support letters, contradicting their finding.
propositions.quote: There is no mention in the Officer’s reasons of the evidence confirming that the Applicant’s tuition has been paid, that further tuition funds are held in trust for her and that her room and board costs are covered, nor is there any reference to the third-party letters from the various professionals confirming the aunt and uncle’s ability to cover her expenses.

propositions.text: This failure renders the Officer's financial analysis unreasonable.
propositions.quote: There was clear evidence that contradicted the Officer’s finding that she had not demonstrated that “funds would be sufficient or available”, which the Officer failed to address. I find that this renders the Officer’s financial analysis unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer failed to address contradicting financial evidence, rendering the financial analysis unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Officer found the Applicant and family not well established in home country and was not satisfied she would leave Canada.
propositions.quote: The documents provided do not show that the applicant or her family is well established in COR or home country. I am not satisfied that the applicant would leave Canada at the end of their stay as a temporary resident, I note that: - the client has strong family ties in Canada (aunt) -the client is single, mobile, is not well established and has no dependents -Currently employed in the UAE since 2019 as Sales, salary and personal funds/assets unknown. Weak professional and economic ties.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found the Applicant and family not well established in home country and doubted she would leave Canada.

propositions.text: The Applicant stated strong ties to the Philippines including family and land ownership.
propositions.quote: The Applicant indicated in her application that her ties to the Philippines were strong given that her father, step-mother and siblings reside in the Philippines and she owns a large parcel of land in the Philippines that she hopes to develop in the future.

propositions.text: She also said her studies would allow time with supportive aunt and uncle in Canada.
propositions.quote: She also indicated that her studies would provide her with an important opportunity to spend time with her aunt and uncle in Canada, who would provide her not only with financial support but also emotional support.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant stated strong family ties and land in the Philippines and support from aunt and uncle in Canada.

propositions.text: Lack of dependents alone should not be a negative factor in study permit applications.
propositions.quote: This Court has repeatedly recognized that an applicant’s lack of a dependent spouse or children, without any further analysis, should not be considered a negative factor on a study permit application.

propositions.text: Officers should not draw negative inferences from family ties in Canada; financial support is a positive factor.
propositions.quote: Moreover, this Court has also held that an officer should not draw negative inferences from an applicant’s family ties in Canada. If anything, an officer should consider the financial support of an applicant’s family as being a positive factor.

propositions.text: Officers must justify reasoning; it is unreasonable to infer illegal stay from strong family ties in Canada.
propositions.quote: At the very least, an officer must justify their reasoning and it is unreasonable to infer that an applicant will remain in the country illegally simply because an applicant has strong family ties in Canada.

propositions.text: The Officer improperly considered lack of dependents and family ties in Canada negatively without justification.
propositions.quote: In this case, the Officer has improperly done all of these things.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer improperly considered lack of dependents and family ties negatively without justification.

propositions.text: The Officer fails to explain how the presence of aunt and uncle in Canada outweighs ties to the Philippines.
propositions.quote: the Officer also fails to explain how the presence of her aunt and uncle in Canada outweighs her ties to the Philippines, where her father and other family resides and she owns land.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the Officer fails to explain how the aunt and uncle's presence in Canada outweighs the Applicant's ties to the Philippines.

propositions.text: The study plan is unreasonable given the Applicant's education and employment history.
propositions.quote: The study plan does not appear reasonable given the applicant's employment and education history.

propositions.text: Applicant's previous studies are at a higher academic level than proposed studies in Canada.
propositions.quote: the client has previous studies at a higher academic level than the proposed studies in Canada (bachelor's tourism)

propositions.text: Proposed studies are not reasonable given career path; career plans are vague.
propositions.quote: the client's proposed studies are not reasonable given their career path. States she would like to upgrade her skills however her career plans are vague.

propositions.text: Motivation to pursue studies in Canada at this point does not seem reasonable.
propositions.quote: Given applicant’s previous educational and employment history, their motivation to pursue studies in Canada at this point does not seem reasonable.

propositions.text: Study plan does not outline a clear career path benefiting from the program.
propositions.quote: Study plan submitted does not outline a clear career path for which such educational program would be of benefit.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found the study plan unreasonable given the Applicant's education, vague career plans, and unclear career path benefits.

propositions.text: The Officer failed to understand reasons for taking Seneca College program as outlined in Statement of Purpose.
propositions.quote: The Applicant asserts that the Officer failed to come to grips with the Applicant’s reasons for taking the Seneca College program, which were clearly outlined in her Statement of Purpose.

propositions.text: Seneca program differs from bachelor's degree, focusing on different tourism industry areas and new skills.
propositions.quote: the Seneca College program was not a repeat of her bachelor’s degree program. Rather, the Seneca College program focuses on an entirely different area of the tourism industry and would provide her with skills and knowledge not yet acquired.

propositions.text: Seneca program includes hospitality and tourism business courses like sales, marketing, customer relations, event planning.
propositions.quote: the Seneca College program has a course in hospitality and tourism that will focus much more on the business side of the industry, including sales, marketing, customer relations, event planning, conventions and conferences.

propositions.text: Seneca program offers knowledge about tourism sectors like cruise ship industry where Applicant has limited knowledge.
propositions.quote: the Seneca College program will permit her to learn a lot more about sectors of the tourism industry in which she has limited knowledge, such as the cruise ship industry.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Officer failed to understand her reasons for Seneca program, which differs from her bachelor's and offers new skills.

propositions.text: Co-op placement is important for hands-on experience and is integral to the program.
propositions.quote: the co-op placement was of particular interest as it would give her real-life hands-on experience in her field. In that regard, the letter of acceptance from Seneca College confirmed that the co-op work placement is an essential and integral component of the program.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant notes the co-op placement is essential and provides practical experience, confirmed by Seneca College's acceptance letter.

propositions.text: Applicant hopes tourism industry recovers post-pandemic to seek employment in Philippines or international settings.
propositions.quote: she is hopeful that the tourism industry will have recovered from the global pandemic by the time she completes her Seneca College program and that she would then be able to seek employment in a new setting, probably in the Philippines or in an international setting, such as with an airline, cruise ship or hotel organization.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant states her future career plans depend on tourism recovery, aiming for employment in the Philippines or internationally.

propositions.text: Officer's failure to address program differences and co-op significance renders that part of determination unreasonable.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s failure to address the differences between the Seneca College program and the Applicant’s bachelor’s program as well as the significance of the co-op program (both of which point to a different conclusion than that reached by the Officer) render this portion of the Officer’s determination unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's failure to consider program differences and co-op importance unreasonable.

propositions.text: Officer's reasons fail to show consideration of entire application and lack justified, transparent basis for refusal.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s reasons fail to demonstrate that the Officer considered the application in its entirety and fail to present a justified, intelligible and transparent basis for the refusal.

propositions.text: Judicial review granted; study permit application remitted for redetermination by another decision-maker.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the application for judicial review will be granted and the study permit application will be remitted back to another decision-maker for redetermination.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's refusal unjustified and grants judicial review, remitting the application for redetermination.

propositions.text: No questions for certification were raised or arise.
propositions.quote: No questions for certification were raised and I agree that none arise.

propositions.text: Judgment grants judicial review, sets aside refusal, and remits application for redetermination by another officer.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is granted. The May 20, 2021 rejection of the Applicant’s application for a study permit by the Visa Section of the Embassy of Canada in Abu Dhabi is set aside and the application is hereby remitted for redetermination by another officer.

paragraphs.summary: The court grants judicial review, sets aside refusal, remits application, and finds no certification questions.
